lead: The anchor, the lines and the dinghy are the gear you handle every day, and the gear most often lost or broken. See each piece yourself at the base, try it, and learn how the briefing wants it used.

sections.title: Sign for what you have seen at the bow

qa.q: What should I check on the anchor and chain before signing for a charter yacht?
qa.a: Go to the bow and see it yourself: ask for the **chain marks** and write their colour code on the form, check the bitter end is lashed with rope you can cut, and photograph a cracked roller or missing pin.

blocks.p: Go to the bow before you sign for the ground tackle: anchor on the roller, chain in the locker. Ask for the **chain marks** and write the colour code on the form: scope is counted by the marks. The bitter end should be lashed with rope you can cut in an emergency, not shackled hard.

Photograph a cracked roller or a missing pin and write it down: damage not on the form is yours at check-out. An anchor that comes up upside down on a twisted chain needs a swivel. A blocked locker drain is cleared. Have the **second anchor** dug out with its warp and shackle. With a rope rode, look for sharp edges where it meets the roller.

sections.title: Test every control, keep hands off the chain

qa.q: Why does the anchor windlass do nothing when I press the foot switch?
qa.a: Usually its **breaker** is off. Switch it on and use the windlass with the engine running, or its current flattens the house battery. If the motor runs but the gypsy does not turn, the clutch is slipping.

lines: Breaker on, engine running, try again

blocks.p: Run the chain out and in from both foot switches and from the remote. Nothing at all usually means its **breaker** is off. Use the windlass with the engine running: its current would flatten the house battery. If the motor runs but the gypsy does not turn, the clutch is slipping: tighten it with the windlass handle, which also frees it to lower by hand.

blocks.rule: Chain is cleared with the windlass stopped, never by hand while it runs.

sections.title: Sand, scope, and a pull to prove it

qa.q: How much anchor chain should I let out in the Mediterranean?
qa.a: With all chain, **4–5 times the depth**, measured from the bow roller, and more for a windy night: in 6 m with the roller 1 m up, about 30 m. Drop it on pale sand, not weed or rock.

blocks.cap: B: pale sand holds. The anchor skids over weed and jams in rock.

blocks.p: With all chain the usual Mediterranean scope is **4–5 times the depth**, measured from the bow roller, and more for a windy night: choose a sheltered bay shallow enough for your chain.

Set the anchor by reversing slowly, then at about 1,500 rpm, watching a transit ashore. For the night give the plotter's anchor alarm the chain out plus a boat length and a margin: 35 m of chain and a 14 m boat make about 55 m. By day an anchored vessel shows a black ball forward, at night the all-round white light.

sections.title: The windlass lifts chain, nothing more

qa.q: Can I leave the anchor chain on the windlass overnight?
qa.a: No: the load goes onto a **snubber** hooked to the chain and made fast to a cleat, with the chain slack on the gypsy behind it. A catamaran uses a bridle to both bows.

blocks.p: At anchor the load goes onto the **snubber**, hooked to the chain and made fast to a cleat, with the chain slack behind it. A catamaran uses a bridle to both bows, which stops her sheering. To weigh, motor slowly up the chain so the windlass lifts only slack. Where old chains foul the bottom, rig a buoyed trip line on the anchor's crown.
Before a passage close the chain stopper, fit the roller pin and switch the breaker off: a kicked foot switch cannot then drop the anchor.

sections.title: Quays, lazy lines, buoys and lines ashore

qa.q: How far from the quay do I drop the anchor when mooring stern-to?
qa.a: About **four boat lengths** off when there are no lazy lines: drop it closer and it never bites. Come in square to the gap, then reverse in.

refs: Base briefing: stern-to with the anchor
Mooring: stern-to in an onshore wind

labels: town quay · gap between two boats

blocks.cap: B: square to the gap, then reverse in.

blocks.p: Without lazy lines you drop the anchor about **four boat lengths** off the quay: closer and it never bites. If the wind turns onshore, take chain in to pull the stern off, ease the stern lines and lift the passerelle. With a **lazy line**, keep its slack out of the water and clear of the propeller while it is walked forward; have gloves and a boat hook that locks. The base wants the boat back on its own berth, on its lazy line, on time.

blocks.p: See how the passerelle fits, and lash it down for passages.

sections.title: Long enough, sound, and guarded from chafe

qa.q: How long should a stern line be for Med mooring?
qa.a: At least a **boat length**, because it goes to the quay and back; add a long line for the shore. Guard it from chafe at the fairlead and the quay edge: chafe, not strain, parts mooring lines.

blocks.p: A stern line goes to the quay and back, so it is at least a boat length; add a long line for the shore. A hard, chafed line is the base's to replace. Count the fenders and have a flat one pumped up.

Tied this way a fender's height changes in seconds. Fenders go where hull and quay meet, higher at a tall stone quay. Chafe, not strain, parts mooring lines: fit a sleeve or a piece of hose at the fairlead and the quay edge.

sections.title: The gear a waiver often does not cover

qa.q: Does the damage waiver cover theft of the charter dinghy and outboard?
qa.a: Often not: theft of the dinghy and outboard is often outside the **damage waiver**, so read the dinghy clause. Lift and lock the dinghy at night, and try the outboard lock's key at the pontoon.

blocks.p: Check the dinghy inflated hard with every valve closed, its drain plug, oars and pump, and the boat's name on the tubes. Read the dinghy clause: theft of the dinghy and outboard is often outside the damage waiver. So lift and lock it at night, and try the outboard lock's key at the pontoon.

fig.title: Outboard, at the pontoon
lines: Tank vent open, bulb squeezed firm
Stops when you pull the kill cord
Moved between boats on a lanyard

blocks.p: An outboard that dies after a few seconds usually has a closed tank vent. Before a beach, stop the motor and tilt it, then row or wade in. For towing, the outboard rides on the pushpit bracket. On davits, pull the plug so rain drains and refit it before launching; before a rough passage take the outboard off, drain the dinghy and strap it tight.
